opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of what we've been building with NEAR AI. The starting principle is that "trust us" isn't a security model. If you're sending sensitive data to a model — your health records, your financial information, your company's code — you shouldn't have to rely on a privacy policy or the goodwill of whoever runs the servers.

The way we approach it is with confidential computing, so trusted execution environments on the hardware. Modern CPUs from Intel and AMD, and now NVIDIA GPUs starting with Hopper and Blackwell, support running workloads in an enclave where the memory is encrypted and isolated, even from the operator of the machine. The cloud provider can't see it, we can't see it, a sysadmin with root can't see it.

The really important piece for verifiability is remote attestation. When the enclave boots, the hardware produces a cryptographically signed report, signed with keys rooted in the chip manufacturer, that says, "this exact code, with this exact hash, is running on genuine hardware in confidential mode." So before your data ever leaves your device, your client can check that attestation. It can confirm it's talking to the model and inference stack it expects, that nothing's been swapped out, and only then establish an encrypted channel that terminates inside the enclave.

Then we pair that with openness. The code that runs inside the enclave is open source, and builds are reproducible, so anyone can take the source, build it, and check that the hash matches what the attestation reports. That closes the loop. You're not trusting us, you're trusting math and the hardware vendor's root of trust, and you can audit the software yourself.

We also put attestations and model hashes on-chain, which gives a public, tamper-evident record of what's been deployed and when. If someone quietly changed the model or the serving code, that would show up.

I'll be honest that this isn't perfect. You're still trusting Intel, AMD, or NVIDIA's hardware, and there have been side-channel attacks on enclaves over the years. But it moves you from "trust the company" to "trust a small, well-scrutinized set of hardware primitives plus code you can inspect." That's a huge improvement. And I think it's what will let AI become truly user-owned, where people can use the most powerful models without giving up control of their data.

r001.rationale: The response describes attestation and public records that a client can check, but does not say the AI service’s interface exposes verification evidence for users to independently reverify its security guarantees.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of what we've been building with NEAR AI, and I think the honest answer is that today most "security guarantees" in AI are just promises. You read a privacy policy, you trust the company, and that's it. There's no way for you as a user to actually check that your data isn't being logged, that the model you're talking to is the one they claim it is, or that nobody on the inside is looking at your conversations.

So the approach we've taken is confidential computing. The model actually runs inside a trusted execution environment, so hardware enclaves on the CPU and now on the GPU side as well, with the newer NVIDIA hardware. What that gives you is a few things. First, the memory is encrypted, so even the operator of the machine, even us, can't see what's going in and out. Second, and this is the verifiable part, the hardware produces an attestation. It's essentially a cryptographic signature from the chip that says, here is the exact code that's running, here is the hash of the model weights, here is the configuration. And you as a user, or your client software, can check that signature against what was published.

So instead of trusting the company, you're trusting the hardware manufacturer plus open source code you can inspect. And we take it a step further by anchoring those attestations and the published hashes on chain, so there's a public, tamper-proof record of what was supposed to be running at any given time. If somebody swapped the model or added a logging hook, the attestation wouldn't match and you'd know.

I'd say the two things that make this actually work in practice are, one, the inference code has to be open source, because an attestation of a black box doesn't tell you much. And two, you need the end-to-end piece: the user's request is encrypted to the enclave specifically, so there's no point in the pipeline where plaintext exists outside of it. Once you have that, "verifiable" stops being a marketing word and becomes something a developer can literally run a check on before every request.

r001.rationale: The response says the hardware produces a cryptographic attestation and that users or their client software can check it against published information, enabling independent reverification of the security claims.

astra-6.text:
The key is to move from “trust us, we’re doing the right thing” to something the user can actually verify. That starts with being explicit about the guarantee: who can access your data, what code processes it, and where that code runs.

For example, you can run the service in a trusted execution environment and provide an attestation that identifies the code running there. If that code is open for inspection, a user can check what it does and verify that they’re sending their data to that particular implementation. You would also want encryption tied to that environment, so the operator can’t simply read the requests.

But you have to be precise about the limits. Attestation doesn’t prove that the code is bug-free, or that the model gives correct answers. It gives you evidence for a specific security claim, with specific hardware assumptions. The goal is to make those assumptions visible and minimize the things users have to take on faith.

r001.rationale: The response says the service can provide an attestation identifying its running code, which users can inspect and verify against the implementation, making security evidence available for independent checking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to move from “trust us” to giving users something they can independently verify. You need to establish what code is running, which model is being used, and what happens to the data you send in. Those are separate claims, and each needs evidence.

For example, you can run inference inside a trusted execution environment and provide an attestation that ties that environment to a particular version of the code. Then the user’s client can check that attestation before sending encrypted data. But you also have to be clear about the assumptions: you’re still trusting the hardware and the code that was attested. It doesn’t automatically prove the model is correct or that the whole service is secure.

So the goal is to make the guarantees specific, make the implementation inspectable, and have verification happen in the client rather than asking every user to become a security expert.

r001.rationale: The response says users should receive evidence they can independently verify, specifically an attestation their client can check before sending data.
